family: ONE THING FOUND OUT IN THE HAND AND NOTHING CHANGED. The hand finds the size of one thing, or finds what a thing is like inside, by span, by roll, by slide, by tip, by press, by thumb; and the whole of what the chapter knows at the end is that finding, and nothing is marked, nothing is cut, nothing is fastened, nothing is filled, nothing is shimmed, nothing is written down and nothing is put right.
why_not_the_nearest: 0065 WAS ONE SOUND SHALLOW FIX ON TIRED GROUND WITH A TOOL. 0066 WAS ONE SOUND SHALLOW KEEP ON GROUND ALREADY MOVED WITH A TOOL. 0067 WAS ONE SOUND LOOSE THING TAKEN IN HAND, LOOKED AT, AND PUT DOWN AGAIN, WITH NO TOOL AT ALL. THE 0067 FINDING WAS MADE BY LOOKING, AND IN NINE OF ITS TEN CHAPTERS THE OBJECT WAS LOOKED AT FROM OUTSIDE THE HAND. HERE THE FINDING IS MADE BY THE HAND AS A GAUGE — the span of two hands, the width of a knuckle, the depth of a thumbnail, the length of a boot — and THE OBJECT IS ONLY THE REASON THE HANDS WERE PUT WHERE THEY WERE. THE MEASURING KIND OF FAMILY IS DIFFERENT FROM THE LOOKING KIND IN THE WAY IT IS DIFFERENT FROM THE FIXING KIND, AND IT IS DECLARED HERE BEFORE ANY PROSE AND NOT CHANGED QUIETLY IN THE CHAPTERS.
family_nearest_turned_away_from: 0065 one sound shallow fix on tired ground with a tool. 0066 one sound shallow keep on ground already moved with a tool. 0067 one loose thing in the hand and no tool at all. NEITHER THE GESTURE, THE DOOR, THE BAND, THE FAMILY NOR THE CLOSING IMAGE IS QUIETLY CHANGED ANYWHERE IN THE TEN.
ten_gestures_and_the_rule_about_them: THE GESTURE IS THE ACTION OF THE HAND AND NOT THE OBJECT, AND NO TWO CHAPTERS MAY USE THE SAME GESTURE. TEN DIFFERENT HANDS. THE TEN HANDS SPENT IN 855 TO 864 MAY NOT BE USED: weighed in the palm, turned in the hand and read on a stone, turned a quarter with the fingers, lifted on the flat of a card, held out at arm's length and looked at edge-on, rubbed along the top face with a thumb, held by the head and shaken once over a sheet, lifted a quarter inch and let back down, drawn out between two fingers, taken off in the hand. TURNED OVER IN THE HAND AND PUT BACK IS BANNED IN EVERY BLOCK SINCE 0066 AND IS NOT USED HERE. THE TEN BELOW ARE ALL NEW.

cards.0865: At the unit a man in his early forties has a board off the top of the stack of spare boards in the yard and means to close his hand across the knuckles of one hand with the board between them and take the width off the knuckles, and then to set that width against the width of the store door opening and find whether it goes across, and to mark nothing.
cards.0866: At number twelve a woman of seventy-eight has six feet of edging in a heap and means to take one stone off it and bring both hands together on it from the two ends until the fingers of one meet the thumb of the other, and to find out how many hands a stone of that heap takes to lay, and to lay nothing.
cards.0867: At the lock-up a woman in her late forties has a kerb at the bay that is not the same width at one end as at the other and means to set both hands at the two ends of it and walk them along until they meet, and to find where it steps, and to set nothing square to it.
cards.0868: At number nine a woman in her late fifties has nine path joints full and the tenth open under a lipped flag, and means to take that tenth flag up and hold it on its edge and draw the two hands apart once to see whether anything gives, and to find how thick that flag is against the other nine, and to relay nothing.
cards.0869: At number ten a woman in her early thirties has the boards off the back wall of the passage and a dry brick off the heap and means to set a thumbnail into the end of a board and lay the other thumb along its face and take the depth off the corner, and then do the same to the brick, and to compare the two and put both down.
cards.0870: At the unit a man in his early forties has the top of the bench and a bundle of stiff cards off the store shelf and means to stand a card on end on the bench and push down on it with one fingertip until it will go no further, and to do that three times, and to find how deep that bench top is, and to write nothing.
cards.0871: At number ten a woman in her early thirties has a ring of chippings banked round the foot of the butt base and means to press the heel of her hand flat against them to find the line where the ground stops the hand, and to walk that ring all the way round, and to find the one place where it is not the same, and to rake nothing.
cards.0872: At the lock-up a woman in her late forties has two lengths of rack bar in the rack and a third lying off it and means to lay the third down beside the two and walk the ends even with the toe of her boot, and to find how short it is, and to put it back off the rack.
cards.0873: At number twelve a woman of seventy-eight has a loop of blue string over the top of the edging heap and means to take it up along the ground in both hands with the slack gathered and walk the hands towards each other along it, and to find how much longer than the heap the loop is, and to untie nothing.
cards.0874: At number nine a woman in her late fifties has a gate post carrying a gate that hangs out over the road and means to put both arms round that post as far as they go and then take them in a hand's width on each side, and to find how much wider the post is than the stile it carries, and to set the gate no differently.

NONE OF THE TEN HAS IT. 3. THE TOOLS-STOWED BEAT IN NO MORE THAN THREE OF THE TEN. IT IS IN 0869 AND 0872 AND NOWHERE ELSE, AND IN NEITHER IS IT THE LAST THING. 4. THE TEN CLOSING MOVES ARE SET BELOW IN THE ORDER OF THE CHAPTERS: a conditional with its time in a subordinate clause; an inventory of two closing on a possessive relative; a negative assertion after a time clause; a place and a time joined by a prepositional phrase closing on a future perfect; a comparison that reverses; a count closing on a relative clause with its time in it; a locative phrase closing on where the dip is; a negative sentence with an exception; a statement of consequence with its time in a subordinate clause; an assertion of cause after a plain statement in a compound.

declared_ordinary_word_note: DECLARED BEFORE ANY PROSE OF 865 TO 874 EXISTS. IT IS NOT DUST, WHICH WAS 0065, NOT EDGE, WHICH WAS 0066, NOT GRAIN, WHICH WAS 0067, NOT A WORD ON THE OLD LIST AND NOT A BAND DECLARE. IT MAY NOT BE hold, holds, holding, held, change, changes, changed, plain, counted, steady, breathed, wrote, nodded, household, threshold, encounter, determine, noticed, notice, exchange, pause, suddenly, finally, realise, realize, seem, seemed, begin, began, watch, watched, garden, shoulder, usually, anyway, almost, nearly, quite, just, kind. WEAR IS THE ORDINARY WORD OF THIS BLOCK AND IT RUNS FOR HOW A THING HAS BEEN USED: THE WEAR ON A KNUCKLE, THE WEAR ON THE TOP OF A KERB, THE WEAR ALONG AN EDGE OF STONE, THE WEAR IN A THREAD OF A RACK BAR, THE WEAR ON A DOOR STILE. IT IS AN ORDINARY WORD AND NOT A FIGURE.
anti_tick_rules_written_before_any_prose: NO CHAPTER ENDS ON A JOB FINISHED AND NONE ENDS ON THE THING BEING PUT BACK. FOUR END ON A THING LEFT AS IT IS AND NOT PUT THERE BY THIS WORK: 0867 THE KERB THAT STEPS, 0868 THE TENTH JOINT THAT STAYS OPEN, 0872 THE THIRD LENGTH LYING OFF THE RACK, 0874 THE LEAF HANGING OUT OVER THE ROAD.

THE SECOND PERSON IS SHOWN AND NEVER REPORTED, EXCEPT THAT THEY MAY BE ASKED A PLAIN QUESTION AND MAY ANSWER IT, AND MAY SAY ONE THING THAT IS NOT ABOUT THE JOB, AND THE PERSON DOING THE WORK MAY ANSWER THAT BACK. NOBODY IS TOLD ANYTHING ABOUT THE WORK, NOBODY REFUSES ANYTHING, NOBODY IS PASSED THE WORK ON AND NOTHING PASSES BETWEEN PEOPLE ABOUT THE JOB.

IN NO CHAPTER DOES THE SECOND PERSON TOUCH THE THING IN HAND OR SEE IT. IN 0865, 0866, 0870, 0871, 0872 AND 0873 THE VISITOR IS ELSEWHERE IN THE YARD OR THE STREET. IN 0867, 0868, 0869 AND 0874 THE MEASURING IS DONE AND THE HANDS ARE EMPTY BEFORE THE VISITOR ARRIVES.
A FIGURE THE CHAPTER ITSELF SETS MUST CLOSE. WHERE A COUNT IS MADE IT IS MADE ONCE AND THE ENDING KEEPS IT. SINGLE-PLACE COUNTS ONLY.
THE TEN GESTURES ARE THE ACTION OF THE HAND AND NOT THE OBJECT, AND NO TWO OF THEM ARE THE SAME, AND THE OBJECT IS NOT WHAT VARIES THE CHAPTER.
THE TEN DATELINES ARE TEN DIFFERENT CONSTRUCTIONS AND THE CLOSER IS IN ONE OF THEM ONLY.
NO WATER IS DRAWN, CARRIED, POURED OR EMPTIED BY ANYBODY AT WORK IN ANY OF THE TEN. THE ONLY WATER IN THE TEN IS RAIN AND THE WEATHER.
NO CEMENT, MORTAR OR NEW CONCRETE IS PUT DOWN ANYWHERE IN THE TEN.
still_live_and_taken_up_by_nobody_here: THE EIGHT SPENT THINGS MAY NOT BE SPENT AGAIN: no moss left in a joint, no tuft of grass left standing in a kerb joint, no band of pale plaster behind a rail, no chipped arris left bare, no old grease left across the foot of a guide, no bright patch on a corner, no worn place on a rail, no joint left unfed because the thing above it is proud. NONE OF THE EIGHT APPEARS IN ANY OF THE TEN, AND THE DECLARED ORDINARY WORD FOR THIS BLOCK IS WEAR AND NOT WORN PLACE.
